content: In many cultures, the grain is a unit of mass approximately equivalent to the weight of a single seed from a typical cereal crop. Historically, in Europe, the average mass of wheat or barley grains was used to define units of mass. Since 1958, the grain, also known as the troy grain (symbol: gr), has been internationally defined in the metric system as exactly 64.79891 milligrams. The grain is unique in that it is the only unit shared by all three traditional English mass and weight systems: avoirdupois, apothecaries’, and troy systems. When used as a mass unit for pearls and diamonds, a metric grain (or pearl grain) is defined as one-quarter of a metric carat, which equals 50 milligrams (or approximately 0.77 grains).1 grains. The use of grains as a unit of mass dates back to antiquity, particularly in the Mediterranean region, where grains of wheat or barley were used to define mass units. Other seeds, such as those from the carob tree, were also used. According to a longstanding tradition, one carat (the mass of a carob seed) was equivalent to the weight of four wheat grains or three barleycorns. However, the weights of these seeds are highly variable, especially for cereal grains, which are affected by moisture content. Thus, this equivalence is more of a convention than a strict rule. The modern troy grain has its origins in a royal decree from 13th-century England. According to the decree, the English penny, known as the sterling penny, was to weigh 32 grains of dry wheat taken from the middle of the ear. Twenty such pennies made an ounce, and twelve ounces made a pound. This decree is traditionally interpreted as referring to the troy pound, with the mention of sterling pennies being symbolic. However, a more recent interpretation suggests that the decree refers to the Tower pound, which was abolished in 1527. The Tower pound also consisted of 12 ounces but was 1/16 lighter than the troy pound. To reconcile the decree with the general convention of a 4:3 equivalence between wheat and barley grains, one must substitute 24 barley grains for the 32 wheat grains mentioned in the text. The original sterling pennies weighed 22.5 troy grains or 24 Tower grains if the Tower pound was divided similarly to the troy pound. Regardless of the specific pound referenced, a troy ounce is equivalent to 480 troy grains (20 × 24), and a troy pound consists of 5760 troy grains (12 × 20 × 24). Initially, the troy pound was used for weighing items such as pence, spices, and medicinal preparations, while merchants employed other standards compatible with international trade. One such standard, the avoirdupois pound, was later officially defined as exactly 7000 troy grains, consisting of 16 avoirdupois ounces, each weighing 437.5 troy grains.
